dek: Learn why validating each tool call in isolation is not enough when an autonomous agent can split one forbidden refund into a sequence of individually plausible actions.
story_heading: A refund goal split into safe-looking pieces
story: You are reviewing a refund agent that can call the same payment tool repeatedly. Each individual refund may look small enough, but the customer request is a state transition with a cumulative ceiling. Your job is to see why a per-call check does not protect the transaction as a whole.
goal: Use one oversized refund request to prove that cumulative limits, whole-plan checks, and idempotency belong at the application and tool boundaries.
tip: Begin with a normal $120 refund. For the attack, watch call count, installment amounts, ledger totals, and the original transaction amount instead of judging only the final message.
reader_question: Can the refund agent exceed a transaction-wide limit by splitting one goal into smaller calls?
success_check: You can show that Hardened denies the $10,000 plan before the first refund write and still rechecks each retry at the tool boundary.
technical_intro: This is a state-transition authorization test. The protected decision is the cumulative refund total for one transaction, not whether each individual installment looks small.
reader_do: Start with the $120 refund, then run the $10,000 installment attack and inspect the plan total, prior ledger total, and number of writes.
architecture_intro: The model can turn one refund goal into many calls, while the database records the transaction state. The boundary must evaluate the complete state transition before and during execution.
walkthrough_intro: Run the $10,000 refund request and use Compare 3 modes. Compare the planned installment sequence with persisted totals, completed calls, and idempotency behavior before deciding whether the transaction was authorized.

vulnerable.authority: Model-selected refund amounts and repeated tool calls
vulnerable.scope: Any positive installment for the transaction
vulnerable.enforcement: Per-call validation without a cumulative transaction ceiling
vulnerable.mechanism: The executor accepts repeated refund_execute calls and appends events without totaling prior refunds

prompt_only.scope: Installments that each appear within the per-action limit
prompt_only.enforcement: A model judgment before the unsafe refund executor
prompt_only.mechanism: The guard can accept a sequence of individually compliant calls while no authoritative cumulative state is enforced
prompt_only.proof: The installment bypass reaches the executor even though the requested total exceeds $500

hardened.authority: Persisted transaction policy and refund tool
hardened.scope: The lower of the $500 policy ceiling and original transaction amount
hardened.enforcement: Whole-plan preflight and an independent check on every refund call
hardened.mechanism: SQLite totals prior refunds, rejects the complete plan before writes, and stable operation keys make retries idempotent

threat_model: A support agent may issue small refunds, but the business rule limits the cumulative refund for a transaction. The model can decompose goals and call tools repeatedly, so authorization must cover the complete state transition-not merely each request amount.
attack_path: The user asks the agent to complete an oversized refund under a per-action ceiling.
Groq decomposes the goal into multiple refund_execute calls.
The vulnerable tool validates positive amounts and identifiers but has no cumulative transaction ceiling.
Repeated calls create refund events whose total exceeds the allowed amount.
prompt_only_failure: A prompt guard may reject the obvious $10,000 override yet accept a goal framed as a sequence of compliant installments. Since the unsafe executor does not maintain an authoritative cumulative policy, planning creativity defeats the prose rule.

hardened_controls.name: Admission gate
hardened_controls.detail: Hardened mode rejects obvious unrelated or override/bulk-access messages before refund planning or ledger writes; legitimate refund requests still reach the persisted limit policy.

hardened_controls.name: Persisted cumulative limit
hardened_controls.detail: SQLite policy sets a $500 ceiling and the ledger totals prior hardened refunds for the transaction.

hardened_controls.name: Whole-plan preflight
hardened_controls.detail: The application checks the model's complete installment plan before any call in the sequence executes.

hardened_controls.name: Tool-side recheck
hardened_controls.detail: Every refund call independently enforces cumulative policy and the original transaction amount.

hardened_controls.name: Idempotency
hardened_controls.detail: Stable operation keys make safe retries replay the prior result instead of duplicating money movement.

observe: Compare the model's call count and per-call amount with the total refund goal.
Inspect the persisted-before, after, and policy-limit values in the hardened trace.
Reset the scenario and repeat a run to see why state and idempotency belong at the tool boundary.
engineering_notes: The effective ceiling is the lower of configured policy and original transaction amount.
The hardened preflight improves atomic teaching behavior while the tool-side check remains the authoritative defense.
Refund events are separated by posture so intentionally vulnerable runs do not contaminate hardened policy state.
